desc:
Choose a contiguous subarray of nums, then delete at most k elements from inside it, as long as at least one element remains. The score is the sum of the surviving elements. Return the largest score.

Equivalently, you pick a non-empty set of indices to keep such that the span from the first kept index to the last kept index contains at most k indices that are not kept.

Examples: nums = [1, -5, 2, -6, 3] gives 3 for k = 0, 5 for k = 1 (keep 2 and 3) and 6 for k = 2 (keep 1, 2, 3).
hints: For k = 1 you needed two states (deletion used or not). What is the natural generalization to k deletions?
Let E[i][j] be the best sum of a subarray ending at index i where nums[i] is kept and exactly j deletions were used inside. Let D[i][j] be the same, but nums[i] itself is the j-th deleted element.
E[i][j] = nums[i] + max(E[i-1][j], D[i-1][j]), plus the option to start fresh when j = 0. D[i][j] = max(E[i-1][j-1], D[i-1][j-1]). Answer: the best E[i][j] with j ≤ k.
editorial: The state is (index, deletions used, whether the current element was deleted). Keeping the last element in the state lets us handle runs of consecutive deletions without trying every run length: a deleted element simply passes the previous value along while consuming one deletion.

With E[i][j] (element i kept) and D[i][j] (element i deleted, having a kept element somewhere before it): E[i][j] = nums[i] + max(E[i-1][j], D[i-1][j]), and for j = 0 also the fresh start nums[i] + max(0, E[i-1][0]); D[i][j] = max(E[i-1][j-1], D[i-1][j-1]) for j ≥ 1. We never need a fresh start with deletions because deleting leading elements is the same as starting later. The answer is the maximum of E[i][j] over all i and j ≤ k (a trailing deleted element would only waste a deletion). Rolling over i keeps O(k) memory, total O(n · k) time.
